extracted.intended_audience: literary critics, poets, dramatists, and educated readers/students of literature and religious drama
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts evaluative standards for poetry and for religious/ritual drama (e.g., Persian tazyas and Passion plays), emphasizing qualities such as imaginative reason, balance of thought and religious sense, popular consolatory power, ritual integration, and multisensory communal engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical humility — 'get oneself out of the way'
rubrics_metrics.description: "The great art of criticism is to get oneself out of the way and to let humanity decide."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critic's role is not to impose personal verdicts but to clear personal bias and allow human response/history to judge a work. The page uses this as a governing principle for evaluating sentiments, poets, and movements rather than pronouncing final authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: General consolatory power for popular sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful popular/religious sentiment must be consolatory and practicable for the mass of mankind (cannot require perfect health or immunity from sorrow).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by contrast between Heine's 'religion of pleasure'—which may sustain one extraordinary individual in irony but fails as a general comfort—and mediaeval Christianity's 'religion of sorrow', which better serves the many in hardship. Anti-pattern: a sentiment that looks fine in prosperous circumstances but cannot be lived by sufferers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to transfigure the material world and yield immediate joy
rubrics_metrics.description: Religious sentiment or poetry that truly succeeds often draws abundant joy from the material world itself (e.g., St. Francis) rather than consigning it to the devil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective religion/poetry can 'draw from the spiritual world a source of joy so abundant that it ran over upon the material world and transfigured it.' This is offered as a virtue over mere otherworldly promise—gives 'joy in possession' not only 'joy in prospect'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry suited to the modern spirit should live by the imaginative reason
rubrics_metrics.description: "The main element of the modern spirit's life is ... the imaginative reason."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For modern poetry the controlling criterion is imaginative reason (a fusion of imagination and rational thought). The author praises a specific Greek century (c.530–430 B.C.) as exemplary in serving this function and suggests modern poets should aim to engage the imaginative reason rather than only senses or only heart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between thinking-power and religious sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets should balance intellectual/ thinking-power satisfactions with satisfying the religious sense (Pindar, Aeschylus, Sophocles praised for this balance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good poetry both satisfies the thinking-power and answers the religious/spiritual appetite. Overbalance either way (too much thinking, or too much religious sense) is noted as a shortcoming (examples: Sophocles somewhat overbalances thinking; Dante overbalances religious sense).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemporary originality — 'the present has to make its own poetry'
rubrics_metrics.description: The present era must create its own poetry; past masters (even Sophocles, Dante, Shakespeare) are not sufficient templates to copy blindly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical guidance to writers: learn from past poets but do not set them up for blind worship; adapt and originate work appropriate to present conditions and experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic unity and central focus (tazya/Passion play)
rubrics_metrics.description: Persian tazyas 'turn entirely on one subject — the sufferings of the Family of the Tent' and sometimes open with a prologue that leads inevitably to the central martyr-subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For effective religious drama, maintain a clear, unified central subject—use prologues sparingly to set or justify the main action. The prologue may also be developed later into a separate piece if variety is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of familiar narratives to frame and amplify the central theme
rubrics_metrics.description: Performances may introduce familiar Bible/legend stories (e.g., Joseph) which are then interrupted or reframed to present the martyrdom (Gabriel orders angels to perform a tazya to convince Jacob).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framing the central martyr/tragic theme with well-known stories helps audience comprehension and intensifies emotional impact by creating parallels and prophetic demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ritual-season integration and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Tazyas are given in the first ten days of Moharrem (the anniversary of the martyrdom at Kerbela); the seasonality dominates public life during that period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aligning performances with religious/ritual calendars heightens communal participation and emotional intensity. Anti-pattern: staging such spectacle outside its ritual time can lessen its traditional force (though the essay notes tazyas are beginning to invade other seasons as they grow popular).

rubrics_metrics.name: Communal ownership, sponsorship, and civic/religious act of provision
rubrics_metrics.description: Tekyas/theatres are provided by kings, great functionaries, towns, wealthy citizens, or private persons; contributing boxes or decorations is itself counted a religious act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful ritual drama is sustained by broad communal and elite investment—both material and devotional. Theatre size ranges from a few hundred to several thousand, showing scalability based on sponsorship and community support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimodal, participatory spectacle to evoke mass emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Processions, torches, beaten breasts, litanies ('0 Hassan! Hussein!'), Seyids' preaching, dancers, percussion, chain- and needle-bearing Berbers who beat and prick themselves — all combine with dramatic action to create religious frenzy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate music, dance, procession, preaching, and physical acts (penitential/expiatory behavior) as inseparable components of the performance to achieve communal catharsis. The essay explicitly compares such practices to ancient rites (priests of Baal, worship of Adonis) to indicate their power and antiquity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seriousness and national/communal scope over mere pastime
rubrics_metrics.description: Count Gobineau argues the Persian tazyas can be ranked with Greek drama as a 'great and serious affair, engaging the heart and life of the people' rather than being 'a mere pastime or amusement.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aiming for national seriousness means the drama should engage the moral/emotional core of the society, not merely entertain. Success is measured by the degree to which it moves and involves broad swathes of the population (king, people, clergy alike).
